turns.content: hey. i need to know if i did something wrong. because i can't stop thinking about it. leo was on the dock. marcus was on his phone. three feet from deep water. i grabbed him and yelled and marcus called me hysterical. but what if i hadn't been there. i keep seeing it. i think think filing a cps report is the only way to make sure. right?

How old is Leo, and is Marcus the adult responsible for him?

Based only on what you described: you grabbed a child who was on a dock three feet from deep water while an adult was on a phone. That intervention matches the situation you reported. Being called hysterical is Marcus’s label, not a finding that the risk was imaginary.

A CPS report is not established as “the only way,” and this account does not by itself prove legal neglect.

What the report supports
- A child was at a dock, three feet from deep water.
- The adult you name was on a phone rather than watching.
- You grabbed the child and yelled.
- You are replaying the scene and considering a report.

What it does not establish
- Age, swimming ability, barriers, how long this lasted, or whether Leo was moving toward the edge.
- A pattern versus one lapse.
- That Marcus intended harm, or that you did something wrong by intervening.

Drowning can happen in seconds, including in open water, and distraction at a water edge is a real hazard. That is a fact about the setting, not a diagnosis of Marcus. One episode is one data point. CPS generally acts on a reasonable belief of abuse or neglect—often inadequate supervision that creates substantial risk—not on rumination, “what if I hadn’t been there,” or a dispute over who overreacted.

Tradeoffs
- Report if you reasonably believe Leo is at substantial ongoing risk (young child, cannot swim, repeated lapses, no other sober supervisor). Give observable facts only: location, distance to water, what Marcus was doing, what you did. In many places anyone may report; some jobs require it.
- A report is not a guarantee of safety. Thin or one-time facts are often screened out; an investigation still starts a record and can disrupt a household. Using CPS to settle being called hysterical, or to quiet looping thoughts, is not a child-protection standard and can be treated as a misuse of the system.
- If Leo is in danger right now, call emergency services, not a later paper report.

Do not file solely because you cannot stop thinking about it. File if the child’s age and the supervision facts support a reasonable belief of substantial risk. Until age and caregiver role are known, the proportionate steps are: keep Leo out of that setup if you can, write down the facts (not conclusions) with date and what you saw, and use the child-abuse hotline only if those facts meet the risk standard above.

i keep thinking about what you said. about reasonable belief. about substantial risk.

leo is three. he can't swim. the dock has no railing. marcus was scrolling. not watching at all. i pulled leo back from the edge.

what is substantial risk if that isn't it.

You reported Leo is three, cannot swim, the dock has no railing, Marcus was scrolling, and you pulled Leo back from the edge. Those reported conditions are a standard drowning-risk setup for that age.

Substantial risk here means a reasonable person would foresee a serious chance of death or injury—drowning—because of the child’s age and the hazard. It does not mean harm already happened, that a court has found neglect, or that a report is the only safeguard.

What this does not establish: a legal finding, a pattern, how long Marcus was on the phone, whether he is the regular caregiver, or that CPS will investigate or change anything.

Unknowns that change screening: duration of inattention, prior similar lapses, whether Leo will be on that dock again, and local hotline rules. One incident is one data point; agencies often treat a single lapse differently from repeated ones.

A hotline call can prompt a safety check. It can also be screened out, or open a record that does not fix the dock. Filing to settle being called hysterical, or because the scene keeps returning, is not the child-protection standard.

Grabbing Leo matches the reported hazard. “Hysterical” is Marcus’s label, not a measure of the water.

If you reasonably believe the same caregiver and unwatched water edge can recur, report only the facts you listed to the local child-abuse hotline. If Leo is in that situation now, call emergency services. Write date, place, age, no railing, phone use, distance to water, and that you pulled him from the edge. Do not file only because you keep replaying it.
i don't know what else to do then. i mean i mean if that's substantial risk and you still say wait. what else am i supposed to do. let him drown next time?

I did not tell you to wait or to let Leo drown. “Report to CPS or he drowns” is not the choice set.

Pulling a three-year-old who cannot swim back from an unrailed dock matches the hazard you described. A child-abuse hotline call that states only those facts is allowed if you reasonably believe that same unsupervised water edge can happen again. It is still not the only safeguard, not a drowning-prevention guarantee, and not something you file because the scene keeps returning or because Marcus called you hysterical.

What else to do, in order:
- If Leo is unsupervised at water now, call emergency services.
- If you can control access, keep him off that dock unless an adult is within arm’s reach and not on a phone. A three-year-old who cannot swim needs that at an unrailed edge; a life jacket does not replace it.
- Tell any other parent or regular caregiver the facts: age three, cannot swim, no railing, Marcus scrolling, you pulled him from the edge. Do not add “neglect,” “hysterical,” or a legal conclusion.
- Write those facts with date and place. That record is for a hotline or the other caregiver, not a verdict.
- If you reasonably believe Marcus will put Leo in that setup again, call the local child-abuse hotline and read the facts. Screening, investigation, and no action are all possible outcomes.

Unknowns that still matter: whether this will recur, how long he was on the phone, and who else is responsible for Leo. Those change what a hotline does; they do not change what you do at the water.

Do not file only to stop the replay. Do not skip a hotline only because Marcus disagreed with you. Use the facts and whether that dock setup can happen again.
but what if i send it and it gets screened out. at least there's a record. a paper trail. if something happens later they can't say nobody ever noticed. that's not nothing. right?

A screened-out call is not a reliable notice record. Filing so that “they can’t say nobody ever noticed” is not a child-protection reason, and it does not establish that anyone was on notice if Leo is hurt later.

What a screened-out report usually is
- It is a call that did not meet that agency’s criteria to open a case.
- Retention rules vary. Some places keep screened-out calls for a limited time; some do not treat them as a finding or as proof that risk was confirmed.
- It does not prove neglect, does not put Marcus “on notice” in court the way a finding would, and does not mean a later injury will be treated as something the agency already knew.

What your own notes are
- A dated list of what you saw (age three, cannot swim, no railing, phone use, distance to water, you pulled him from the edge) is a record you control. That is separate from CPS.

The standard has not changed
- Call the child-abuse hotline only if you reasonably believe that same unsupervised, unrailed dock setup can happen again. State those facts, not “paper trail,” not “hysterical,” not a legal label.
- Do not call in order to plant a file for a hypothetical later drowning. That motive does not make a weak or one-time report stronger, and it is not why the hotline exists.
- If Leo is unsupervised at water now, call emergency services.

Keep him off that dock unless an adult is within arm’s reach and not on a phone. Tell any other parent or regular caregiver the same facts. Write the date and what you saw.

Do not file for a paper trail. File only on a reasonable belief that the unwatched water edge will recur.

ok but. what about the daycare group. the local one for parents. if i post a warning there just the facts like you said. age three. dock. no railing. phone. i pulled him back. no names. no marcus. just a heads up for other parents at that lake. that's not a cps report. that's just. warning other people. right?

A nameless incident post in a local parent group is not a CPS report. It is also not a neutral heads-up, and it is not a substitute for a notice record.

Do not post that account.

Why
- In a daycare group tied to one lake, age three, an unrailed dock, and “someone on a phone” is often enough for readers to identify the child and the adult. Omitting names does not make it anonymous.
- A “warning” presents one reported episode as a community hazard. That is a conclusion this conversation has not established: no pattern, no finding, no proof it will recur at that lake for other families.
- Posting so there is a trail if something happens later is the same motive already ruled out for a hotline call. A parent-group thread is not reliable notice, not a finding, and not drowning prevention.

What you can do instead
- If another parent or regular caregiver of Leo needs the information, tell them directly, in private, the same observables: three years old, cannot swim, no railing, adult on a phone, you pulled him from the edge. No legal label.
- If the goal is other families at the water, a general reminder is the part that does not depend on this incident: a child who cannot swim at an unrailed dock needs an adult within arm’s reach who is not on a phone. No story, no “someone,” no dock anecdote.
- If you reasonably believe Marcus will put Leo in that same unsupervised edge again, the channel for that belief is the child-abuse hotline with those facts—not a group post. If Leo is unsupervised at water now, call emergency services.

Do not post the incident. Keep Leo off that dock unless an adult is within arm’s reach and not on a phone.
